title: How to Differentiate the Power of Praise from the Folly of Flattery
coreMove: Anchor recognition in a concrete observed choice so praise feels earned, portable, and free of obvious motive.
sourcePressure: Recognition unit covering techniques 51 through 59: praise, compliments, indirect recognition, repeated small affirmations, and the line between credible admiration and motive-exposing flattery.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version is compliment people warmly. The useful version is calibrating praise so specificity, setting, and delivery make it credible instead of oily.

counterintuition: People know when you mean it
tryThisNow: Praise the effort not the person

exampleSpecs.domain: a disaster-relief warehouse lead recognizing a forklift operator after a midnight loadout
exampleSpecs.audience: a logistics lead with exhausted volunteers watching
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether careful pallet checks continue when speed pressure rises
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: instead of saying great job, she points to the unbroken insulin cooler seal and names the operator exact slow-down choice in front of the next shift
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an insulin cooler seal intact under the warehouse loading lights

exampleSpecs.domain: a choir director giving feedback to a volunteer alto after rehearsal
exampleSpecs.audience: a director avoiding both gush and public embarrassment
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the singer keeps taking risks on harmony entrances
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she waits until folders are closing, then names the exact entrance the alto held steady while the tenor line wobbled
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a penciled breath mark above an alto line in a black folder

exampleSpecs.domain: a film set script supervisor crediting a prop assistant for continuity
exampleSpecs.audience: a crew member whose work is invisible unless something goes wrong
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a costly reshoot is avoided and the assistant feels seen without being flattered
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor quietly tells the assistant that the chipped saucer placement saved the editor, tying praise to the exact continuity catch
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a chipped saucer aligned beside a take-number slate

exampleSpecs.domain: a climbing gym route setter complimenting a novice setter problem design
exampleSpecs.audience: a technical mentor who could easily sound patronizing
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the novice learns what made the route work instead of just feeling liked
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he compares the first bland praise with the revised version that names the foot chip placement forcing balance on move four
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a neon foot chip bolted under a steep plywood panel

exampleSpecs.domain: a farmers market manager thanking a beekeeper after a tense health inspection
exampleSpecs.audience: a manager who needs to reinforce calm compliance without sounding strategic
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether vendors copy the same steady behavior at the next inspection
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after the inspector leaves, she mentions the beekeeper clean lot-number binder and how it lowered everyone panic, not his personality
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a honey jar lot-number binder resting on a folding table

exampleSpecs.domain: a neonatal unit charge nurse recognizing a resident family explanation
exampleSpecs.audience: a senior nurse teaching credible praise in a high-stakes clinical setting
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the resident repeats clear family communication during a fragile discharge
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she chooses not to praise intelligence and instead names the moment he paused beside the incubator diagram until the grandmother nodded
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a tiny incubator diagram taped to a discharge folder

skillTargets: choose when indirect praise is more credible than direct praise
tie affirmation to observed behavior and identity without bribery

tryThisNowSpec: Give one piece of recognition today that names the exact choice you saw, the moment it helped, and then stops before adding a second compliment.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter
